This is the absolute LAST post I ever expected to be making on the Monday of my bodybuilding show week.

After months of weighing every gram of food, tracking every calorie, hitting my workouts, doing my cardio, practicing my posing, and preparing myself mentally, physically, and spiritually to step on stage this Saturday, I spent this past weekend binge eating in a way I’ve never experienced before.

And when I say binge eating, I don’t mean I went out and enjoyed a cheat meal or ate a little more than I was supposed to.

I mean I completely lost control.

I kept eating long after my stomach was telling me to stop. I was physically uncomfortable, I wasn’t even enjoying the food anymore, and yet I continued eating.

And the scariest part wasn’t even the amount of food I consumed.

It was what was going through my head while I was doing it.

At a certain point, it felt like I was intentionally sabotaging myself. Like there was a part of me that wanted to ruin everything I had worked so hard for.

And I’ve spent the last couple of days asking myself WHY.

Was I afraid I wasn’t going to look good enough on stage? Was I afraid of disappointing myself? Was I putting so much pressure on myself that I subconsciously wanted a way out?

I don’t have all the answers.

But those are some uncomfortable questions I’ve had to start asking myself.

After the first binge, I told my coach Chris Elkins everything. Every single thing I ate. We talked about it, and the plan was to move forward, reassess, and take things day by day.

The next day, I got right back to my routine. Tracked my food, followed my plan, and genuinely thought I had moved past what happened.

Then nighttime came.

What started as one extra bite of food turned into another binge. And this one was even worse than the first.

I can’t even explain how disappointed I felt afterward.

Not because I had eaten food that wasn’t on my plan. But because I had reached a point where I felt like I couldn’t stop myself from doing something I knew was hurting me.

I woke up physically miserable. My face was extremely swollen, my body felt awful, and I was looking at myself in the mirror trying to understand how I had gotten here.

And now here I am.

Five days away from the competition I’ve spent months preparing for, roughly 10 pounds heavier than I was going into the weekend, and genuinely uncertain whether I’m going to step on stage this Saturday.

Chris believes competing is still an option. Part of me wants to finish what I started. Another part of me wonders whether postponing until November would be the better decision.

Because I know how much work I put into this prep. And I also know that the choices I made this weekend have consequences.

I’m not going to sit here and blame anybody else. I’m not going to pretend it didn’t happen. And I’m definitely not going to ask anyone to feel sorry for me.

But I also don’t want to spend the rest of my life beating myself up over two days.

I made those choices. I have to own them. And now I have to figure out how to move forward.

One thing this weekend has forced me to recognize is just how much pressure I’ve been putting on myself. Not only with bodybuilding, but with life in general.

Constantly working. Constantly thinking about what’s next. Constantly being on my phone. Constantly feeling like I need to be doing MORE.

And somewhere along the way, I stopped giving myself enough room to just live.

So regardless of whether I compete Saturday or in November, some things are going to change.

I’m prioritizing my sleep. I’m taking real breaks from social media. I’m giving myself time to recover. And I’m going to take a serious look at my relationship with food and the pressure I’ve been putting on myself.

I’m not going to pretend I’ve figured everything out in 48 hours. I haven’t.

And I don’t want to turn this into some inspirational story about how I fell down and immediately got back up stronger than ever.

I’m still figuring it out.

Pero cuando Dios nos conceda la victoria, los mismos que hoy dicen todo eso cambiarán su discurso. Dirán que siempre fue fácil, que cualquiera podía hacerlo, que las pandillas de Haití no eran tan peligrosas como se pensaba.

En fin, nunca los hemos escuchado y no vamos a empezar ahora.

Todos los que se han enlistado son creyentes y hemos encomendado esta misión a Dios, mientras que las pandillas de Haití son satánicas y es de conocimiento público que hacen sacrificios humanos.

Dios nos concederá la victoria. El Creador del Universo está con nosotros.

¿BUKELE Y SU WATERLOO?

Con el anuncio del envío hacia Haiti, desde El Salvador, de un contingente de 3000 militares, cuya misión es encontrar a los 4 miembros de las fuerzas armadas de ese país, secuestrados el pasado domingo, cuando penetraron en territorio dominado por las pandillas y fueron atacados por una pandilla de irregulares armados, se avizoran en las próximas horas fuertes enfrentamientos armados.

A estas horas, y sabiendo cómo se resuelven las cosas en Haití, las probabilidades de que estos militares continúen vivos son mínimas, así que si no hay posibilidad de negociar nada, y por lo tanto lo que se plantea es un enfrentamiento armado entre tropas de El Salvador y las pandillas que son dueñas del territorio donde fueron atacados y secuestrados los militares centroamericanos.

Según lo publicado en la prensa internacional, los responsables son dos organizaciones criminales que dominan el área de “Croix des Bouquets”, una de ellas dirigida por Claude Celestin, quien es cabeza de la pandilla Chen Mechan (perros rabiosos), y Wilson Joseph (“Lammo San Jou) líder de la banda 400 Mawozo.

En el día de ayer, este último desafió públicamente  al presidente Nayib Bukele en un vídeo publicado en las redes sociales, donde advirtió que no se irá de Haití, y mostró miles de municiones y pertrechos con arma de diversos calibres, que según el están esperando a los salvadoreños.

Before they died, late Access Bank co-founder Herbert Wigwe and the wife, Chizoba, bought a yacht, which was a shiny toy for them. 

The yacht was named after their first daughter, Otutochi, who ironically is the person today managing the vast wealth that the parents left behind on behalf of the surviving siblings who are younger than her. 

The yacht was a 2016 Custom Line 108 luxury yacht measuring approximately 33 meters (108 feet) in length, and the cost of acquiring it was $6.5 million. 

The yacht primarily served Herbert, his wife, and his close friends anytime they wanted to escape from the reality of the daily life hustle by relaxing and sailing  on the sea. 

The yacht was also deployed for charter for big boys and girls who can afford to rent it. 

The yacht was purchased in 2016, and to escape the wahala that comes with tax, an offshore company, Grosvenor Marine Ventures Ltd., a company registered in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), was incorporated. 

The offshore company was owned by the late Herbert and the wife, and the offshore company's only asset was that luxury yacht. 

Herbert is no more, the same with the wife.

Tochi, the 26-year-old finance graduate who is the heiress to the wealth that the parents left behind, is struggling to maintain the luxury yacht.

The annual cost to own and maintain a luxury yacht typically ranges from 10% to 20% of the vessel's initial purchase price

Main Expense Categories

Crew Salaries: Often the single largest expense, scaling from a small self-operated team to full-time staff costing anywhere from $300,000 to over $1.4 million for mid-size vessels and $1.5 million to $4 million+ for superyachts. 

Routine Maintenance & Upkeep: Accounts for 2% to 10% of the yacht's value annually (covering engine servicing every 100–200 hours, bottom paint, hull cleaning, and HVAC repairs). 

Periodic dry-docking and major refits are required every few years. 

Fuel: Varies heavily by engine power and usage. Larger motor yachts can burn hundreds of gallons of diesel per hour while cruising, easily running into $400,000 to $1 million+ a year. 

Berthing & Dockage: Marina slips range from $30,000 to over $500,000 annually depending on the vessel's length and the prestige of the port (e.g., Mediterranean vs. local marinas). 

Insurance: Comprehensive marine, hull, and third-party liability (P&I) policies cost roughly 0.5% to 2% of the yacht's total value per year (spanning from $30,000 to $500,000+). 

So since the parents died, Tochi has been struggling to keep up with the cost because the asset in question is a depreciating asset. 

At the beginning of this year. She made the difficult decision to sell the yacht because the estate the parents left behind can no longer afford to maintain it. 

It is taking too many resources from her and the estate she is managing on behalf of her surviving siblings. 

But there was a problem. 

The offshore company that her parents floated was no longer active, as it had been dissolved because, since the parents died, the offshore company has stopped filing at the jurisdiction it was registered in. 

So Tochi had to approach  the High Court of Justice of the British Virgin Islands (BVI) to secure control of a company holding a luxury yacht belonging to her late parents.

She also paid the necessary debt the offshore company was owing before the status of the company was restored for the transaction of the sale of the luxury yacht to be completed. 

The luxury yacht was sold in Florida for the sum of $6.5 million, and the money remitted to the estate that Tochi is controlling on behalf of her siblings 

$6.5 million is 8.7 billion naira. 

Herbert  was a very wealthy man in his lifetime. 

I wonder how he managed to stay under the radar that the public did not know he was this wealthy until he was no more.

I’m sure Tochi would have been astounded by the staggering wealth that the late dad left behind....👇
